pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 47. Market closed. Bowls sold: 0. Dumplings eaten: too many. Red envelopes received: 1.*

The market was dark. The lane sat in a silence so thick it felt like a forgotten school hall after the last bus had left. We had to clean the apartment top to bottom before the New Year. Ma sprayed the windows with a mist that smelled of pine, and I wiped the ancestor shelf at the end of the corridor. It was a small wooden box, but it felt like the center of the room.

We placed fresh oranges there, their skin bright and waxy. Ma lit the incense, and the thin white smoke curled up, vanishing into the air. Then we put out Agong’s photograph. He looked young in it, smiling with a gap in his teeth. I wiped the dust from the glass frame, careful not to touch his face.

The doorbell rang. Ba was home. He stood in the hallway, huge and tired, his face red from the wind. He held a bag of oranges in one hand and a whole silver fish in the other. He smelled of diesel and cold air.

"I am hungry," he said, dropping his keys in the bowl. "And the goat story is ready."
pages.image: A small wooden ancestor shelf in a narrow corridor, holding a framed photo of a smiling man, fresh oranges, and burning incense with thin smoke, while a tired father in a work jacket stands in the doorway holding a fish.

pages.text:
"Nián yè fàn," Ma said, pointing at the empty table. "We must fold dumplings for wealth."

I rolled out the dough, but it stuck to my fingers like wet glue. Ama stood in the corner with her arms crossed, watching us with a critical eye. She did not help with the rolling. She only folded. Her hands moved so fast they were a blur, while my single dumpling looked like a sad, lumpy pillow. Ama had already made forty. They sat in a row like little white boats ready for a race.

Ba sat on a stool, peeling an orange. He began his story about his truck. A goat had run into the highway, unafraid and proud. It jumped onto the bumper, and Ba drove for ten kilometers with a passenger in the front seat. The goat ate his sandwich.

"The goat did not pay for the sandwich," Ba said seriously.

Ama stopped folding. She looked at Ba, then at me, and started to laugh. It was a deep, rumbling sound that shook her whole body.

"More fish," she said. "We need the surplus."
pages.image: A cluttered dining table with a large bowl of dumplings and a steamed fish, where a grandmother with silver curls folds dough quickly while a young girl struggles with a messy dumpling and a father peels an orange. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
Ba and Ama started talking, not in Mandarin but in the faster, softer Hokkien that Ama had been speaking to me my whole life. It rolled over smooth vowels and sounded a lot like the water running off our plastic stools when we hosed them down. They discussed the fish, the price of oranges, and the ache in Ba’s bad back.

I tried to listen, but the words slipped through my fingers like wet sand. I wanted to join in, so I opened my mouth, but my tongue felt thick and clumsy, like it had been stuffed with cotton. I tried to say *xièxie*, but it came out as a squeaky *shii-shii*. I closed my mouth immediately, and my face began to burn hot.

Ama looked at me. She did not smile, exactly. She just waited, her eyes kind but firm, watching me the way I watched a dumpling that refused to seal.

"Ama," I said, in my best Hokkien, which sounded like a cat clearing its throat. "I want to learn."

Ama stopped chewing. She looked at me for a long second, then burst out laughing so hard she had to put down her chopsticks and lean on the table to catch her breath.

"Not now," she wheezed. "Eat your fish."
pages.image: An elderly woman with silver curls and a floral vest leaning forward laughing heartily at a dinner table, while a young girl with a green jacket looks embarrassed and a large man in a work shirt smiles warmly in the background. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
After the bowls were cleared, Ama reached into her vest pocket. She pulled out a red envelope. It was bright, the color of luck. She held it out with both hands, palms flat, a perfect gesture I had seen in photos but never practiced.

I took it with both hands, mirroring her. My fingers felt stiff. Inside, there was money. It was an even number, a lucky amount. But tucked behind the bills was a small slip of paper.

I unfolded it. Two characters were written in ink that had slightly smeared. They were shaky, but bold.

*Chia̍h-pá.*

Eat until you are full.

I looked up. Ama was already looking away, pretending to arrange the fruit on the table. But I saw her hands shaking, just a little. It must have taken her an hour to write that. She does not like to write. She does not like to say the big things.

So she wrote the small thing. The most important thing.
pages.image: A close-up of two hands holding a red envelope, with a small piece of paper pulled out showing handwritten characters, while an elderly woman in the background adjusts oranges on a wooden table.

pages.text:
I sat on the balcony wrapped in my green jacket. The city was loud. Fireworks popped and hissed over the rooftops, turning the night sky purple and gold. The market lanterns still hung above the street, dim but bright enough to see the cars passing by.

I held the red envelope in my pocket. I could feel the paper against my thumb.

I had never told Ama that the stall smelled like the best thing in the world. I had not told her I loved the steam. I had not told her I liked the noise or the counting. I had only said I wanted it to look modern. I had only said I was embarrassed.

I breathed in the cold air. It tasted like gunpowder and old wood.

I will tell her tomorrow, I thought. I will say it all tomorrow.

I did not know that tomorrow was a long way away. Some things do not wait for the right day.
